description: Editorial description of the on-screen teaching sequence; not spoken narration. The soundtrack is music.

segments.text: A Transformer block is a repeatable unit combining attention with a feed-forward network.
Attention mixes information across positions, giving each position a context-dependent representation.
A residual connection adds a sublayer’s output to its input, preserving a direct path through the block.
Layer normalization computes statistics over the feature coordinates of each token independently.
For the example [2, −1, 4, 3], mean is 2 and variance is 3.5. Standardization is followed by a learned scale and bias.
The feed-forward network transforms each token separately. This example expands width 64 to 256, applies GELU and projects back to 64.
The second residual connection adds the feed-forward result back to the residual stream.
Pre-norm places normalization before the sublayer; post-norm places it after the residual addition.
Small training comparisons illustrate how normalization placement and warmup can affect optimization. Their outcomes depend on experimental conditions.
Stacking blocks lets later layers build on contextual features produced by earlier layers.
Pause and distinguish operations that mix positions from those that mix feature coordinates within a position.
Recap: attention, residual paths, normalization and the feed-forward network work together. The next lesson assembles complete blocks into a language model.
